candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest classifies this binary as malware with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top SHAP features push toward cryptojacking. The individual contributions are modest (+0.0067 to +0.0152), so the verdict comes from the consistent direction across many features rather than from one dominant signal. The strongest group is stack-manipulation n-grams: SUB PUSH (+0.0152), MOV PUSH (+0.0123, frequency 0.0376), MOVZX PUSH (+0.0115), CALL PUSH (+0.0106), ADD PUSH (+0.0102, frequency 0.0325), PUSH CALL (+0.0088, frequency 0.0291), LEA PUSH (+0.0087) and POP PUSH (+0.0084). Together they point to heavy push-based argument passing and frequent call sequences, which fits large, call-dense compiled code. A second group is rare, unusual sequences: POP SUB, POP XCHG, POP XOR, POP TEST, PUSHFD POP, CALL RET, POP CALL and CDQ MOV. These occur at very low frequency (0.000014 to 0.000230) but carry relatively high SHAP weight (+0.0067 to +0.0146). Such sequences are atypical of ordinary compiler output and can indicate hand-written or obfuscated code, stack or flag juggling, or packer/loader stubs. A third group is arithmetic and numeric patterns: DIV MUL (+0.0067), MOV FLD (+0.0072, frequency 0.0025) and LEA MOVSD.REP (+0.0068). These suggest integer and floating-point computation and block memory copies, which are consistent with compute-intensive or buffer-handling routines like those in mining workloads. No function-level locations were provided, and none of these n-grams is uniquely diagnostic of mining on its own. The conclusion therefore rests on the model's unanimous, saturated prediction and the combined pattern of obfuscation-like rare sequences and compute-oriented sequences, not on direct proof of mining logic. I rate it high-confidence with a moderate-to-high score because of this limitation.

A call immediately followed by a return is a thunk or wrapper pattern, also seen in stub or trampoline code. It is rare (0.000054) but strongly weighted.
Extremely rare (0.000014). POP followed by XCHG is non-standard compiler output and suggests manual register or stack manipulation, possibly obfuscation.
Frequent (0.0291) standard argument-then-call pattern. It reinforces the call-heavy, push-based structure that contributes to the prediction.
Saving the flags register and popping it into a general register is uncommon in normal code. It is sometimes used in anti-analysis, flag inspection or low-level tricks.
Very rare. Popping a value into a register and then XORing it can indicate decoding or register-zeroing in stub or obfuscation code.
Pushing a computed address, typical of passing buffer or structure pointers to functions. Contributes to the overall call and data-handling profile.

Loading a value into the x87 FPU stack indicates floating-point computation, consistent with numerically intensive routines. It is not diagnostic of mining by itself.
Address computation followed by a repeated string move indicates bulk memory copy or initialization, consistent with buffer or state setup.
Popping into a register and then calling can indicate indirect calls or position-independent or stub-style control flow.
Division followed by multiplication suggests modular or scaling arithmetic, consistent with computation-heavy code. It is rare (0.000054) and weakly suggestive on its own.
Common epilogue or register-restore pattern (0.001311). It has low individual specificity and contributes only cumulative weight.
